overview: Balts is a broad name for related Baltic-speaking peoples east and southeast of the Baltic Sea, not one kingdom. These two map labels cover 700 to 1100, with local examples from different centuries. Their outlines are overbroad, extending into areas inhabited by Finnic-speaking communities. They should not be read as exact ethnic borders or as the borders of modern Lithuania and Latvia.

periods.title: Earlier mapped communities
periods.summary: The “Balts” layer covers this century; seventh- to ninth-century Grobiņa offers evidence of local and overseas connections.

periods.title: Regional communities and networks
periods.summary: The later “Baltic tribes” label includes the period of the ninth- and tenth-century Latgalian settlement at Āraiši.

sections.title: Neighbours and people on the move

items.text: The lower Daugava was home to Livonians, who spoke a Finnic language. The Daugava Museum dates their settlement there from the tenth century and describes a culture shaped by Baltic, Scandinavian and other contacts. Living beside the same river did not make everyone speak the same language.

At Grobiņa in western Latvia, Curonian communities encountered settlers from Scandinavia during the seventh to ninth centuries. The Ālande River connected the area with the Baltic Sea, while nearby farmland helped support people. This was a place of agriculture and exchange as well as overseas travel.

Some jewellery from Scandinavian-style graves at Grobiņa also shows Baltic influences. Archaeologists compare objects and burial practices to investigate contact between communities. A borrowed design can reveal an exchange of ideas, although it cannot tell us every detail of its wearer’s identity.

sections.title: A wooden world preserved by water

items.text: Ninth- and tenth-century Āraiši was a fortified Latgalian settlement in a lake. Waterlogged layers preserved timber buildings and objects that usually rot away. Excavators studied a thick accumulation of occupation remains, allowing them to reconstruct much more than the outline of a few postholes.

Āraiši produced wooden bowls and unfinished bowl blanks. The unfinished pieces are especially useful: they show a stage in making a container, not simply the finished result. Woodworkers could turn pieces of a tree into objects needed for serving, storing and handling everyday supplies.

Bast shoes also survived at Āraiši. Bast is fibre from the inner bark of trees, so this footwear connects clothing with knowledge of local woodland materials. Objects that might seem too ordinary to save can become rare evidence when wet ground protects them.

The archaeological park describes Āraiši’s inhabitants as farmers, livestock keepers, craftspeople and traders who also hunted, fished and practised forest beekeeping. Getting food involved several kinds of knowledge. The forest supplied more than firewood, and the lake was more than a defensive moat.

The houses standing at Āraiši today are reconstructions. Their builders used excavated structural details and replicas of ancient tools. This lets researchers and visitors explore how a building might work at full size, while keeping the distinction between surviving archaeological wood and newly built houses clear.

A comb from Kretuonys barrow 52 in eastern Lithuania had teeth on both sides and separate pieces held together. Researchers date it broadly from the ninth century into the early second millennium. Its surviving parts reveal careful small-scale manufacture for an everyday grooming tool.

Woven bands could add both strength and decoration to clothing. Latvia’s heritage inventory records fragments from as early as the sixth century and especially elaborate examples from Latgalian and Livonian areas in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Those later examples extend beyond this map period, showing the craft’s continuing history.

Children appear in the archaeological record too. A study of eastern Lithuanian cemeteries found that many eighth- to eleventh- or twelfth-century children’s burials were inserted into older mounds. Their treatment differed from earlier practices. Burial choices reveal community customs, but cannot measure how much individual parents loved their children.

Small amber pendants shaped like combs occur in seventh- to ninth-century Curonian graves, including Lazdininkai and Palanga. They usually have a suspension hole and carved or incised teeth. These were wearable objects rather than full-sized hair combs. Their exact symbolic meanings remain interpretations, even when the craftsmanship is easy to see.

sections.title: Words that survive from a later century

items.text: No surviving Baltic-language text from 700 to 1100 provides a phrase to quote here. A much later witness is the Old Prussian greeting “Kayle rekyse”, translated “Hello, mister!” in a scholarly study. It appears on folio 63ra of Basel manuscript F.V.2 beside a text dated 1369. This is one Baltic language in Latin letters, not a common language spoken by every group on the map.

ending.text: Neither 800 nor 1100 marks a collective disappearance. Communities followed different political and cultural histories. Baltic languages continue in Lithuanian and Latvian, while other historical languages were lost or survive only in limited records.
